Question: Harold made a plum pie to take on a picnic. He was able to eat only \(\frac{1}{4}\) of the pie, and he left the rest for his friends. A moose came by and ate \(\frac{1}{3}\) of what Harold left behind. After that, a porcupine ate \(\frac{1}{3}\) of what the moose left behind. How much of the original pie still remained after the porcupine left?
Solution:
Each animal eats a fraction of the pie that is left at that moment. It is convenient to track the fraction remaining after each step.

Harold leaves \(1-\frac14=\frac34\) of the original pie. The moose eats one third of that remainder, so it leaves two thirds of it. The porcupine then also leaves two thirds of the new remainder. Thus the fraction of the original pie still present is

\[
\frac34\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac23=\frac13.
\]

The answer is \(\boxed{\frac13}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\). Multiplying the successive fractions remaining keeps track of the changing whole.
